source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1360-0443.2010.03344.x (Addiction 106(4):787-788, free access), read in this reader's own browser tab (tab-7, opened and closed by me; no other tab touched, nothing downloaded): the four running-text paragraphs, the declaration of interests, the author's affiliation and all 18 references. Statements about Halpern et al. (2011) checked against PMC3053129.

design.note: A four-paragraph commentary published beside the study it discusses; narrative-review is the nearest schema value and the design_detail says plainly what it is. Four paragraphs, 18 references and 'Declaration of interests: None' all confirmed.

instrument.note: none-applicable with the editors' narrative-review checklist (METHODS §5.3).

key_findings.note: 1st paragraph, as printed: 15 tests 'reported previously by others to differentiate ecstasy users from controls'; only the RSAT a clear indication of poorer performance, in heavy but not moderate use; selection for low exposure to other illicit drugs and alcohol; controls from the same rave subculture; adjustment for demographic factors and ADHD; 'the most informative retrospective study to date'.

2nd paragraph. Small point for the editor: the commentary's own words are 'higher impulsivity on a neuropsychological test in ecstasy-naive individuals predicted subsequent ecstasy use'; 'decision making' comes from the title of its reference 12 (Schilt et al., 2009), as the card says.

3rd paragraph: 'yet the evidence remains mixed [4-7,13]'; fenfluramine transporter deficiencies years later (ref 15) against apparent recovery with abstinence in people who use ecstasy (ref 16); and the statement that the two possibilities cannot be disentangled in retrospective studies.
4th paragraph and references 17-18: ref 17 is Ludewig et al., Biol Psychiatry 53:205S (a supplement abstract) and ref 18 Mithoefer et al. (2010), the pilot randomized trial in PTSD.

reporting_issues.note: Halpern's Table 3 gives the non-dominant-hand pegboard difference in the heavier subgroup at p=0.003, the same p as the RSAT difference, and the Discussion calls it likely chance on exploratory analyses.

Reference 16 is Thomasius et al. (2003), 'Mood, cognition and serotonin transporter availability in current and former ecstasy (MDMA) users', a single-time-point comparison; 'recover with abstinence' is an inference from it.
Reference 17 is a one-page supplement abstract and reference 18 a pilot trial; neither sample size nor any neurotoxicity measure can be read from the commentary.

domains.note: some-concerns is right: the design of the study under discussion is appraised carefully, and nothing else is.

I would accept high here too, since the closing sentence treats two small studies as grounds for calling the whole question a chimera, but some-concerns is defensible because the trait argument is explicitly offered as a possibility.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. A null result in 52 people (22 in the heavier subgroup) with no effect sizes, plus a conference abstract and a pilot trial, is presented as support for the absence of harm.

missed: The fenfluramine argument, which is a third of the commentary, rests on reference 14, a legal and technical book (O'Donnell, Drug Injury: Liability, Analysis and Prevention, Lawyers & Judges Publishing, 2005), for the statements that the drug reduces brain serotonin in animals at lower effective doses than MDMA, that it was prescribed to tens of millions and that it was withdrawn in 1997. Under METHODS §3.1 a book is not a source for an empirical claim, so this should be on the card.

The sentence that 'for political reasons there has been far more interest in MDMA users than in fenfluramine users' carries no citation; it is the commentary's one piece of motive attribution and sits in the paragraph the editors cite.

The commentary does not mention Halpern's equivalence analysis (that study's Table 4), although that is the quantitative basis for a claim that no functionally significant neurotoxicity was found: in Table 4 a medium effect (d 0.5) is excluded on at most 6 of 14 measures, strictly on 5, with the remainder from 0.53 to 0.76.
